title: Mpemba effect in a chemomechanical model of the Kinesin molecular motor
abstract: The Mpemba effect, wherein a system prepared farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one initially closer to equilibrium, has been extensively investigated in a wide range of physical systems. In contrast, its role in biologically relevant non-equilibrium processes remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate anomalous relaxation in the six-state chemomechanical network model of the Kinesin molecular motor under both equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions. We first establish the existence of the Mpemba effect in chemical equilibrium and show that many of its qualitative features can be understood from the underlying free-energy landscape. We then examine the effects of mechanical and chemical driving, showing that breaking detailed balance primarily reshapes the Mpemba phase diagram without qualitatively altering the relaxation phenomenology over the physically relevant parameter regime. Finally, we demonstrate that the relaxation of the motor velocity also mirrors the anomalous relaxation of the underlying stochastic dynamics, thereby identifying an experimentally accessible signature of the Mpemba effect. Our results establish molecular motors as a promising baseline for studying anomalous relaxation in living systems and suggest a broader framework for exploring the Mpemba effect in non-equilibrium biochemical networks.
summary: The paper investigates the Mpemba effect in the Kinesin molecular motor using a detailed chemomechanical network model. By analyzing how relaxation occurs under non-equilibrium driving (load or chemical imbalance), the authors demonstrate that this anomalous relaxation signature is directly measurable through the motor's velocity. This establishes molecular motors as a powerful platform for studying non-equilibrium physics in living systems.
main_problem: The study investigates the Mpemba effect—anomalous relaxation where a system farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one initially closer—within biologically relevant, non-equilibrium processes.
main_result: The authors establish that the Kinesin motor model exhibits the Mpemba effect in chemical equilibrium, and crucially, they show that this anomalous relaxation signature can be directly observed via the motor's velocity, even when mechanical or chemical driving breaks detailed balance.
method: The analysis employs a six-state chemomechanical network model governed by a master equation formalism. Relaxation dynamics are quantified using spectral decomposition criteria (like $a_2$) and distance metrics ($	ext{L}_1$).
model_or_system: The system is the Kinesin molecular motor, modeled as a six-state kinetic network. The dynamics are controlled by external load force ($F$) and chemical driving parameters ($c$), which break detailed balance from equilibrium.
key_observables: Motor velocity ($v(t)$), $	ext{L}_1$ distance to steady state, and spectral coefficients ($	ext{a}_2$).
important_parameters: External load force ($F$), chemical driving parameter ($c$), and temperature/energy barriers.
main_assumptions: The model assumes separation of time scales for internal conformational fluctuations (Kramers' analogy) and that the motor velocity accurately reflects the underlying stochastic dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the network states, the Mpemba crossing phenomenon in this context, steady-state velocity dependence on load/driving, and how force quenches affect spectral criteria.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model's equilibrium behavior. It then analyzes non-equilibrium driving (load/chemical) to show that while these break detailed balance, they preserve the qualitative Mpemba phenomenology. Finally, it demonstrates that the measurable motor velocity mirrors this anomalous relaxation signature.
why_interesting: This work applies concepts from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (like transient dynamics and relaxation rates) to a complex biological machine, providing a concrete, experimentally accessible physical manifestation of an abstract thermodynamic phenomenon.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Panel (a): The chemo mechanical network representing Kinesin motion. This numbering of states will be used throughout. F is the forward cycle and B is the backward cycle, directed along the arrows. Panel (b): Schematic of Kinesin walker on a microtubule undergoing mechanical and chemical transitions. Panel (c) shows that the Kinesin system initially equilibrated at a higher temperature relaxes faster than the same initially equilibrated at a lower temperature, yielding Mpemba crossing.

Figure 2: Non-equilibrium nature of the Kinesin depicted by the velocity defined via the current. Panel (a): Steady state velocity v vs load force F, showcasing v decreasing with increasing load and stalling at Fstall = 0.8. Other parameters are Tb = 1, s = 0.5, r = 0.1, c = 0.1, θ = 0.6. Since c ̸= 1, the network is out of equilibrium. Panel (b): Velocity v vs chemical driving c for Tb = 1, s = 0.5, r = 0.1, F = 0. c = 1 corresponds to chemical equilibrium, resulting in v = 0.

Figure 3: Examples illustrating equivalence of the spectral a2 condition with the Mpemba effect. Panel (a): Distance to steady state as a function of time for steady states prepared at Tc = 1.5 & Th = 20, showing a Mpemba crossing at a time tc. Parameters are Tb = 0.4, r = 0.1, s = 2.5.
